Family Health

Feeling lightheaded: what to do and when to get help

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Feeling lightheaded often means you may faint. Sit or lie somewhere safe first. Some episodes pass quickly, but repeated symptoms or warning signs need assessment, and treatments for an inner-ear disorder are not general remedies for faintness.

Lightheadedness, dizziness and vertigo describe different feelings

Lightheadedness usually means feeling as though you may faint. You may feel weak, heavy or unsteady, with blurred vision, nausea or sweating. Dizziness is a broader everyday word that can include this sensation, imbalance or a false sense of movement. Explain the feeling in your own words rather than worrying about choosing the perfect medical term.

Vertigo means that you or your surroundings seem to move when they are not moving that way. It may feel like spinning, tilting, swaying or floating. A sensation of impending fainting and a spinning attack can overlap, but they do not necessarily have the same cause or treatment.

Get into a safe position first

Stop what you are doing and sit or lie somewhere safe before you fall. If you feel about to faint, lying down with your legs raised may help; if that is not possible, sit with your head lowered. In later pregnancy, lying on your side is preferable. Get up gradually after the feeling passes.

Do not keep walking, climb, drive or use machinery to see whether you can push through it. If someone has collapsed, check responsiveness and breathing and call emergency services if they do not respond normally or are not breathing normally. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions. Never give food or drink to someone who is unconscious or cannot swallow safely.

Warning signs that need emergency care

Seek emergency help for lightheadedness with significant bleeding, chest pressure or pain, severe breathlessness, collapse or signs of a stroke. Stroke signs include sudden facial droop, one-sided weakness, difficulty speaking, visual loss or a severe unexplained headache. Sudden neurological symptoms remain urgent even if they improve.

Heart-related symptoms may also include unexplained sweating, nausea or vomiting, especially with chest discomfort or shortness of breath. A pounding or irregular heartbeat with fainting, a faint during exercise or while lying down, serious injury, seizure-like movements or incomplete recovery also needs immediate assessment. Call for help rather than driving yourself to hospital.

A blood-pressure drop can happen on standing

When you stand, your circulation normally adjusts to maintain blood flow to the brain. If blood pressure falls too much, you may feel faint or have dimming vision. This is called postural or orthostatic hypotension. Standing quickly can bring the symptoms on, and sitting or lying down may ease them.

Dehydration, illness, some medicines and other conditions can contribute. A brief improvement after lying down does not establish the diagnosis or rule out another cause. Repeated episodes deserve review, particularly if they cause falls or happen despite getting up slowly.

Illness, dehydration and food intake can contribute

Fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, heat and heavy sweating can reduce fluid availability. Not drinking enough while unwell may add to the problem. Colds and flu may be accompanied by weakness or dizziness, sometimes because of dehydration and sometimes because an inner-ear problem follows an infection.

Low blood glucose is another possibility, particularly for someone taking insulin or certain diabetes medicines. It is not the explanation for every episode in someone who has missed a meal. Iron-deficiency anaemia and other health problems can also produce similar symptoms, so repeated spells should not be treated only with snacks and water.

Anxiety, substances and medicines are relevant history

Anxiety or panic, including fear triggered by heights, can come with lightheadedness. Breathing too fast or too deeply can contribute through hyperventilation. That does not mean every episode is psychological. New breathlessness, chest pain or fainting should not be dismissed as anxiety without considering other causes.

Alcohol, nicotine and recreational drugs can contribute to dizziness or impaired balance. Prescription and non-prescription medicines may also be involved, particularly after a new medicine or dose change. Some antihistamines, sedatives, anti-nausea medicines and blood-pressure treatments can cause drowsiness or a blood-pressure drop.

Allergy symptoms or medicines taken for them may be part of the history, but an ordinary allergy is not a diagnosis for unexplained collapse. Faintness with swelling of the tongue or throat, wheezing or severe breathing difficulty can be an emergency allergic reaction. Tell the clinician about all substances and products without stopping prescribed treatment abruptly.

Serious causes can resemble an ordinary dizzy spell

An abnormal heart rhythm or a heart attack can reduce effective circulation. Internal bleeding may be less visible than bleeding from a wound, and major blood loss can cause shock with dangerously low blood pressure. Stroke and other neurological conditions can also affect balance or produce sudden dizziness.

The sensation alone cannot distinguish these conditions from a less serious cause. Use the associated symptoms and clinical assessment, not an assumption that feeling better briefly means everything is safe. Significant bleeding, severe pain, worsening weakness or a new neurological change should change the urgency of seeking help.

Why the inner ear can cause spinning and imbalance

Balance depends on information from the eyes, the inner ears and sensors in muscles and joints. If the signals conflict or one system is not working well, the brain may perceive movement or have difficulty maintaining balance. Inner-ear disorders are a common cause of vertigo, but central nervous-system causes also need consideration in the appropriate setting.

Tell the clinician about hearing loss, ear pressure, ringing, headache and whether head movements trigger brief attacks. Ménière’s disease, positional vertigo and migraine-related dizziness are different conditions. An examination, hearing assessment or other tests may help distinguish them. A list of treatments for dizziness does not mean they suit every one of these diagnoses.

Fluids and glucose help only in the right situation

If you are alert and can swallow, drink suitable fluids when dehydration is likely. Ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea may call for an oral rehydration product; severe dehydration or inability to drink may need supervised intravenous fluids. IV fluids are a medical treatment, not a routine upgrade for a brief dizzy spell.

If you have diabetes and symptoms of a hypo, check glucose if possible and follow the agreed low-glucose treatment plan promptly. Fast-acting carbohydrate may be needed, followed by reassessment and further food according to that plan. Sugary drinks are not a universal treatment for lightheadedness, and no oral treatment is safe during reduced consciousness.

Fluid requirements depend on health, activity and losses. Follow any heart or kidney-related fluid restriction rather than forcing eight glasses or a large volume at once. Recurrent symptoms despite reasonable intake need assessment, not simply more water.

Do not start water tablets or restrict salt as a general remedy

For selected people with Ménière’s disease, a specialist may discuss a diuretic and changes to dietary salt. This advice concerns a particular inner-ear disorder. It should not be carried over to ordinary faintness or postural hypotension.

Amiloride is a diuretic, sometimes called a water tablet; naming it in a dizziness article does not make it the right medicine for you. Diuretics and unnecessary salt restriction can worsen some low-blood-pressure or dehydration problems. Ask for advice specific to the diagnosis, and do not change a prescribed fluid or salt plan independently.

Nausea, migraine and anxiety treatments need a purpose

Some medicines provide short-term relief from vertigo or nausea, while migraine prevention may help when migraine is the underlying cause. These are separate decisions. A medicine that reduces nausea may also cause sleepiness and increase the risk of a fall.

Diazepam, sometimes called Valium, and alprazolam, sometimes called Xanax, are benzodiazepines. They can cause sedation and dependence and are not routine self-treatment for feeling faint. A clinician must weigh any specific indication and duration. Psychological therapy may help when anxiety contributes, alongside assessment and treatment of other causes.

Balance rehabilitation is a tailored treatment

Vestibular rehabilitation uses selected exercises to help the balance system adapt and improve function. It can be useful for certain ongoing vestibular problems and may be part of a plan to reduce falls. A trained professional chooses exercises according to the diagnosis and limitations.

It is not simply an instruction to repeatedly provoke severe dizziness on your own. In Ménière’s disease, rehabilitation is used for chronic imbalance rather than to treat the acute attack itself. Positional manoeuvres for some forms of vertigo are another distinct intervention and should be matched to an appropriate assessment.

Ear injections and surgery are specialist options

For selected difficult-to-control Ménière’s disease, gentamicin may be injected into the middle ear so it affects inner-ear balance function. This is not treatment of an ordinary ear infection. It deliberately reduces vestibular activity and carries a risk of hearing loss and persistent imbalance, which must be discussed beforehand.

Labyrinthectomy is an irreversible operation that removes or disables inner-ear sensory function. It is reserved for carefully selected severe cases, usually after less destructive treatment has failed and hearing in that ear is no longer usable. Recovery may require compensation and rehabilitation. Neither this operation nor an ear injection belongs on a routine treatment list for faintness.

Reduce the chance of an injury while seeking answers

Move slowly, pause between lying, sitting and standing, and ask for help if walking feels unsafe. A properly chosen walking aid may be useful after assessment. Remove loose rugs and trailing electrical cords, keep routes clear, use secure non-slip bathroom surfaces and make sure the home has adequate lighting.

If a spinning attack makes bright light uncomfortable, a quiet dim space may help while you rest safely. Sunglasses may improve comfort outside, but avoiding bright light is not a universal way to prevent lightheadedness. Do not make walkways so dark that falls become more likely. Close your eyes only when safely seated or lying down, not while trying to walk.

Avoid driving and hazardous work during symptoms. If episodes are recurrent or involve loss of consciousness, ask about local driving rules and when it is safe to return. A temporary improvement does not automatically make driving appropriate.

Regular meals, rest and support can help daily life

Eat regular balanced meals and drink according to your needs and medical advice. Avoid smoking and substances that worsen symptoms. These steps support general health, but they do not replace treatment of anaemia, a heart problem or a vestibular condition.

Sleep needs vary by age. General guidance recommends eight to ten hours for teenagers, at least seven hours for adults aged eighteen to sixty, seven to nine for ages sixty-one to sixty-four and seven to eight for older adults. Persistent fatigue or poor sleep deserves attention rather than treating a target number as a cure for dizziness.

Relaxation, gentle breathing, counselling or suitable yoga and meditation may help with stress. Avoid forceful repeated deep breaths if you are already hyperventilating, and avoid positions or exercises that risk a fall. Support for anxiety is useful without implying that symptoms are imagined.

Get reviewed when the pattern persists or changes

Arrange medical advice if symptoms keep returning, do not settle, worsen or interfere with daily activity. Any actual faint should be reviewed, even after recovery. Do not wait a full week, for an injury or for nausea to appear before seeking help. Sudden severe symptoms or warning signs require a faster response.

Bring a medicine list and note timing, duration, triggers, recent illness, bleeding, pregnancy possibility and associated symptoms. Assessment may include pulse, blood pressure in different positions, examination and selected tests. The aim is to treat the cause and agree on follow-up, while keeping you safe from falls in the meantime.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The words dizziness and lightheadedness cover different experiences. Timing, triggers and associated symptoms help guide assessment.

Fluids, glucose, medicines, rehabilitation and procedures have different indications. No single remedy fits every dizzy spell.

How BeMama can help

Record what the sensation feels like and what happens immediately before it. Bring that account and your medicine list to the appointment.

When to seek help

Primary-care, neurology/ENT and country-specific emergency and driving review remain pending. Chest symptoms, significant bleeding, stroke signs or concerning collapse need emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Sit or lie down promptly rather than risk a fall.
  • Do not assume every episode is low blood sugar or anxiety.
  • Specialist vertigo therapies are not routine faintness treatments.
  • Recurrent symptoms deserve review without an arbitrary one-week wait.

Frequently asked questions

Is lightheadedness the same as vertigo?

Not necessarily. Feeling about to faint differs from a false sensation of spinning or movement, although people may call both dizziness.

Should I stay standing until it passes?

No. Sit or lie somewhere safe. If about to faint, lying with legs raised can help; later pregnancy calls for side-lying.

Do I need to wait a week before asking for help?

No. Repeated, persistent or worsening symptoms warrant advice sooner, and warning signs need urgent or emergency assessment.

Does improving after lying down prove it is harmless?

No. It can fit a blood-pressure drop, but does not establish the cause or rule out a serious problem.

Should everyone drink something sugary?

No. Fast-acting carbohydrate is used for low glucose in the right setting. Never give food or drink to someone who cannot swallow safely.

Will eight glasses of water cure it?

No fixed amount is a cure. Fluid needs and restrictions vary, and the underlying cause may be unrelated to dehydration.

Are amiloride and a low-salt diet standard treatment?

No. Selected inner-ear conditions may have a specialist diuretic or salt plan; these measures can worsen some causes of faintness.

Can I take a sedative to stop the dizziness?

Do not self-treat with one. Sedation, dependence and falls are important risks, and treatment must match the diagnosis.

Are ear injections and surgery options for ordinary faintness?

No. They are reserved for selected vestibular disorders, with risks including hearing loss and lasting balance effects.

Does anxiety mean no physical assessment is needed?

No. Anxiety can contribute, but new symptoms, recurrent episodes and warning signs still need appropriate assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
